analysis.one_liner: Bans grocery sellers from using personal data and algorithms to charge individual shoppers different prices.
analysis.headline: Rep. Chris Pappas introduced the bill in April 2026, but it has no cosponsors and has not moved since being referred to two House committees.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would prohibit retailers from using automated systems and surveillance data — like purchase histories, location data, or purchased consumer profiles — to set a customized price for a specific shopper on food and groceries. Loyalty card discounts would stay legal as long as eligibility rules are disclosed, applied uniformly, and the data is not reused for other purposes like profiling or targeted ads. Enforcement would come from the Federal Trade Commission, state attorneys general, and private lawsuits with minimum damages, and shoppers could not be forced into arbitration to enforce it.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who buys food. The bill targets surveillance-based pricing, in which stores use data about an individual shopper to decide what price that shopper sees. By banning that practice for groceries, it keeps the posted price the price everyone pays, and it gives shoppers legal remedies — including $3,000 per violation, attorney's fees, and access to court rather than forced arbitration — if stores use surveillance data to set individual prices anyway.

how_it_helps.text: The bill bans 'surveillance-based price setting' — using an automated decision system to offer a customized price to a specific person or group based on surveillance data, which includes observed behavior, biometrics, genetic information, and any data gathered or purchased from others.

Stores may still offer discounts through loyalty, membership, or rewards programs, and to groups like teachers, veterans, seniors, and students — but only if eligibility criteria are clearly disclosed, the discount is offered uniformly to everyone who qualifies, and the surveillance data is used solely to administer the discount, not for profiling, targeted advertising, or individualized pricing.

Before offering these discounts, stores must publish procedures allowing consumers to correct or challenge inaccurate data and must disclose what data the automated system considers when setting prices.

Violations are treated as unfair or deceptive practices under the FTC Act, with the FTC empowered to enforce even against common carriers and nonprofits; state attorneys general can sue on residents' behalf, and individuals can sue for the greater of actual damages or $3,000 per violation, with awards up to triple that for willful violations and attorney's fees for prevailing plaintiffs.

Pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers between grocers and consumers would be invalid for claims under this section, so shoppers could go to court instead of being forced into individual arbitration.

analysis.who_pays: Grocery retailers, including major chains, and the data-broker and adtech firms that sell shopper profiles would give up a pricing tool — the ability to charge different individuals different amounts based on data about them — and would bear compliance costs, disclosure requirements, and litigation exposure.

drawbacks.text: The effect on actual grocery prices is uncertain: surveillance pricing can charge some shoppers more, but individualized pricing can also lower prices for price-sensitive shoppers, so a ban could lead stores to keep prices uniform and, in some cases, uniform may mean higher for everyone than the personalized rate would have been.

The definitions are broad. 'Surveillance data' includes any data 'gathered, purchased, or otherwise acquired,' and 'personal information' covers any attribute that could reasonably be linked to a person or household — which could sweep in ordinary practices like using a shopper's own loyalty-card history, and expose retailers to litigation over ordinary operations.

The private right of action with $3,000 minimum statutory damages per violation, multiplied to triple for willful violations, creates a lawsuit exposure for food sellers — a cost that may be passed to shoppers — and compliance with the disclosure and data-accuracy procedures imposes administrative costs on smaller grocers as well as chains.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — that the price you see at the shelf should not depend on a data profile of you — is a clear consumer protection, and the carve-outs for loyalty discounts and disclosed group discounts preserve most common ways shoppers get lower prices today. The real drawbacks are breadth and litigation risk: the definitions could reach routine retail data practices, and statutory damages invite suits whose costs retailers may pass on. On balance it is a targeted consumer protection with real but manageable design flaws, and its bigger weakness is that it has drawn no support, so its protections exist only on paper.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 2026 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Judiciary committees, where it has sat with no cosponsors, no hearings, and no votes as the session continues.

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Pappas (D-NH) introduced the Lower Grocery Prices Act on April 9, 2026.

The bill was referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and in addition to the Committee on the Judiciary — a dual referral that means two committees would each need to act on the parts in their jurisdiction for the bill to reach the floor.
No other action has been taken: no cosponsors have joined, no committee has held a markup or hearing, and the full House and Senate have not voted on it.
The 119th Congress remains in session through January 3, 2027, so the bill is technically alive but has made no progress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: With no vote and no committee action, nothing has changed: retailers and data-broker firms remain free to use shopper data in automated pricing, and shoppers have no new federal protection. Nothing in the record identifies active opponents — the bill simply has not attracted support.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Grocers and data brokers, for now

for.name: Rep. Chris Pappas
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 9, 2026; no other member has cosponsored it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has no cosponsors and no recorded votes or recorded opposition, so no partisan lineup has formed; it simply sits in committee with a single Democratic sponsor.

industries.note: The bill removes their ability to use automated systems and shopper data to charge individual customers different prices, and imposes disclosure, data-accuracy, and litigation obligations. Shoppers' interest in a uniform posted price runs directly against a retailer's ability to extract more from shoppers the data says can pay more.

The bill covers data that is 'gathered, purchased, or otherwise acquired,' so profiles bought from data brokers could no longer feed into grocery pricing. Their business model profits by selling personal data, which is exactly what the bill excludes from pricing decisions.

industries.industry: Loyalty program operators (grocery chains' rewards programs)
industries.note: The bill expressly permits loyalty, membership, and rewards discounts, so grocery chains can keep collecting shopper data through those programs — as long as the data is used only to administer the discount. This keeps loyalty-card data collection as the permanent channel for grocery discounts while barring its use for individualized prices or profiling.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors, a single sponsor, and two committee referrals with no movement after introduction, the realistic path is that the bill dies quietly in committee when the 119th Congress ends in January 2027, unless it attracts cosponsors or a committee takes it up — neither of which has any record of happening.
